newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs welcome Bonn approval of post-war accord.
newsitem.headline: Czechs welcome Bonn approval of post-war accord.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel on Thursday welcomed the Bonn parliament's overwhelming approval of a joint post-war accord, but analysts said the deal faced a rougher ride in the Czech parliament.

The German parliament backed the Czech-German declaration, meant to cement post-war reconciliation, by 578 votes to 20 with 23 abstentions. The accord still needs the backing of Czech deputies in a vote expected early next month.

Havel's press spokesman said in a statement the president welcomed the German parliament's vote on the accord, which was signed in Prague last week by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus after two years of talks.
"The president firmly believes that the declaration will be accepted by both houses of parliament of the Czech Republic," the statement said.

In the accord, Bonn expresses regret for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its sorrow for brutality in the post-war expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans. The text also includes German support for Czech membership of the European Union.
"Above all acceptance of the declaration itself is at stake, the president considers it to be an important step in building good relations among European nations," the statement said.
However, the accord remains highly controversial in both countries. The Czech parliament is expected to approve the declaration but the strength of support is uncertain.
"It will gather more votes against it (than in Germany) but I think the majority will be comfortable," said Bela Plechanovova, lecturer in international relations at Prague's Charles University.
Klaus's ruling coalition is in a minority in the lower house but has a big majority in the Senate upper house.

Czech Foreign Minister Jozef Zieleniec called for the Czech parliament to approve the accord with as big a majority as possible. "It is important that the Bundestag approved it with so many votes ... and it is an appeal to us, to our parliament," he told a news conference.
However, the main Czech opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) have still not clearly stated whether they will support it.
Party leader Milos Zeman visited Bonn this week to discuss adding a rider to the accord, on the grounds that the text does not acknowledge the legal validity of the Czechs' actions.
Czech communists and far-right Republicans also oppose the declaration, insisting it means a loss of Czech sovereignty.

The Czech Republic is seen as a leading candidiate to join the EU and the North Atlantic treaty Organisation (NATO). But after years of Nazi occupation and Soviet domination, many Czechs are suspicious of joining alliances.
Senate chairman Petr Pithart also acknowledged the discussion in the upper chamber would be lively.
"I don't see any great problem, but I expect a deep discussion with controversial opinions, and through this I expect a larger majority (voting in favour) than in the lower house," he told Reuters.
Relatives and supporters of the Sudeten Germans, mostly living in the German state of Bavaria, saying the deal provides no compensation for confiscated property.
Pithart said that despite its problems, the important thing was that a single text had been agreed by both sides.
"As a text it has a lot of problems, but as an expression of common will it is a surprisingly good document," he said.
